DOCUMENTATION / FIELD MANUALINTRODUCTION

IMSISting

A field manual for the 2G · 3G · 4G · 5G cellular research toolkit

Edition for version 1.0.81

What this document is

A description of what IMSISting contains and how to use it, written after the code rather than before it. Every verb named here exists in the tree, every store named here is written by a module named here, and every refusal quoted here is a refusal the toolkit actually performs. Where a capability is absent, the absence is stated in the place a reader would expect the capability to be.

What this document is not

It is not a guide to breaking the law, and it does not pretend the toolkit is harmless. IMSISting transmits on licensed spectrum. Several modules reach a verdict only after a radio in your hand has radiated: a catcher that accepts an attach, a twin that a phone answers, a downgrade that a handset obeys. Running any of those against infrastructure you do not own or have not been authorised to test is an offence in most jurisdictions and, more practically, it is how a research toolkit acquires a legal history that ends its usefulness.

The rule the toolkit itself follows, and the rule this manual assumes: know which of your verbs transmit before you press them. The interface says so — a card that radiates carries a TRANSMITS chip, and the module behind it refuses configurations that would radiate by accident — but the decision is the operator's, not the software's.

How to read this manual

The manual is ordered by the questions a new operator asks, not by the order the code was written:

Part Question it answers
1. Orientation Why is the toolkit shaped this way?
2. Getting it running What do I install, and what does my first hour look like?
3. Interfaces Where do I type, click and read? The CLI, the TUI, the GUI.
4. Catalogue What is this thing? Every module by category, every drawer tab, the target panel.
5. Technique reference How do I actually do it? One page per attack and per passive analysis.

Part 4 never tells you how to run anything and Part 5 never explains what a module is for; they cross-reference each other by section number. A reader who wants to know whether the toolkit can do a thing should read Part 4. A reader who already knows and wants to do it should read Part 5.

Conventions

Convention Meaning
modules/07_gsm_attack.sh --selftest A command you can type. Paths are relative to the repository root.
--verb A verb of the module currently under discussion.
loot/<module>/ A store directory. Stores are append-only TSV unless stated otherwise.
exit 3 A handoff, not a failure. See §1.2.
bold A word the toolkit uses in a specific sense, defined in §1.4.
Selftest: 357 The number of assertion rows the module's own --selftest passes, quoted from a run on a machine with no radio.

Three words carry the whole honesty doctrine of this toolkit and are defined early because the rest of the manual is unintelligible without them: measured, advertised and unobserved. A measured fact came out of a device or a capture. An advertised fact is what a network or a configuration claims about itself. An unobserved dimension is grey, and grey is a legitimate answer — it is not the same answer as "clean".

Parts 1 to 5 of this manual were written by hand. No page of it is generated from the source tree, which is a deliberate cost: a generated page can never drift from the code but also never explains why the code is shaped that way. The gate suite described in §3.4 is what keeps the underlying claims true.
